prompt.context: Our client, Vitality Insurance, is a leading provider of supplemental insurance products in the United States. Vitality agents partner with companies to offer their employees optional, supplemental insurance for such conditions as life, long-term disability, etc. Vitality has undergone fairly steady growth in the past two years, but profit margin is decreasing.
prompt.question: What should Vitality do about its declining profit margin?

clarifying_info.q: How large is Vitality and how do they sell?
clarifying_info.a: Vitality is the leader in its category and has over 10,000 field sales agents. Vitality sells all policies through its field sales agents who are solely compensated on a percentage commission of total new premium, defined as premium from new customers or additional premium (up-sell) from existing policyholders.

clarifying_info.q: Are there sales contests or other incentive programs?
clarifying_info.a: In addition to the standard commission, short-term priorities are often communicated via sales contests that focus on a particular customer segment or activity and pay a bonus in addition to standard commission.

clarifying_info.q: What are the major cost categories?
clarifying_info.a: Major costs are: sales, general and administrative (G&A), and advertising.

clarifying_info.q: What is the competitive environment like?
clarifying_info.a: Vitality has a few other competitors in this market who have seen similar growth, but Vitality is the leader in the space. Competition is not the primary focus.
This is a mature market. Agent turnover is very high on a yearly basis, though it was lower during the recessionary period.

exhibits.title: Vitality Results and Major Costs
exhibits.shows: A table of Vitality's key financial results and major cost line items for 2008, 2009, and 2010 (figures in 000s).

exhibits.title: Vitality Insurance Sales Process and Contest Mix
exhibits.shows: A diagram of Vitality's sales process showing leverage points (Hire new agents, Acquire new accounts, Keep accounts active, Upsell active accounts, Produce results / Premium $, Reactivating dormant account) and the number of sales contests targeted at each leverage point by year (2008, 2009, 2010).

exhibits.title: Snapshot of Sweeps Week Contest Results
exhibits.shows: A line chart showing weekly premium as a ratio to average weekly premium (2008-2010 baseline = 100%) for weeks 1-27 (January through June), with separate lines for years 2008, 2009, and 2010. Two 'Sweeps Week' contests in 2010 are labeled at approximately weeks 4 and 20.

data.y_axis: Ratio to Average Weekly Premium (2008-2010), range 0% to 200%+
data.observation: 2010 line spikes sharply during Sweeps Week weeks; surrounding weeks show below-average premium

framework: Diagnose the profit margin decline: revenue trends vs. cost trends
Break down costs by line item (G&A, Sales, Advertising) to isolate the driver
Focus on abnormal sales cost growth: calculate year-over-year growth rates and compare to premium growth
Analyze the sales incentive structure: standard commission plus contest layer
Map the contest mix shift from 2008/09 to 2010 using the sales process value chain
Evaluate effectiveness of new contests: are they generating incremental premium or gaming behavior?
Assess 'Sweeps Week' specifically: does the spike in those weeks come at the expense of surrounding weeks?
Assess the new-account-focused contests: do they improve or hurt unit economics?
Synthesize: are increased sales costs justified by increased profitability?
Recommend: eliminate or restructure contests that are duplicative or incentivize gaming

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 1, calculate the year-over-year growth rates for premium and each cost line item. What stands out?
questions.guidance: Strong candidates quickly identify that G&A and Advertising grow at roughly 10% per year (in line with premium growth of 10%), but Sales costs grow at 10% from 2008 to 2009, then spike 45% from 2009 to 2010 while premium only grows 10%. This immediately flags sales costs as the culprit for margin compression.

steps: Profit margin declined from 9.4% (2009) to 8.5% (2010), confirming the cost increase is not offset by revenue gains
math.answer: Sales costs grew ~45% from 2009 to 2010 while premium grew only 10%, directly causing the margin decline from 9.4% to 8.5%.

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 2, what changed in Vitality's sales contest mix between 2008/09 and 2010? What does this suggest?
questions.guidance: In 2008 and 2009, contests were spread across multiple activities (acquire new accounts: 2, keep accounts active: 4, upsell: 1, produce premium: 2). In 2010, contests for 'keep accounts active' dropped to 0, while 'acquire new accounts' doubled to 4 and 'produce results/premium' doubled to 4. This signals a strategic shift toward new customer acquisition and total premium volume — both of which are more costly activities than retaining or up-selling existing customers.

questions.prompt: One of the 2010 premium-focused contests was 'Sweeps Week,' which paid an extra 10% bonus on all premium booked during two specific low-volume weeks. Using Exhibit 3, evaluate whether this contest achieved its goal.
questions.guidance: Exhibit 3 shows that the 2010 line spikes dramatically during Sweeps Week (weeks 4 and 20), but the weeks immediately before and after show below-average premium relative to the 2008/09 baseline. This pattern suggests agents were 'gaming' the system — pulling forward or pushing back sales into the bonus weeks to earn the extra commission, rather than generating genuinely incremental premium. The contest boosted volume in the target weeks at the expense of surrounding weeks, producing no net new premium but incurring the extra 10% bonus cost across all booked premium in those weeks. Strong candidates also note that this contest's objective (driving total premium) is duplicative with the standard commission structure, so it adds cost without adding strategic value.

math.setup: 'Sweeps Week' paid an extra 10% bonus on all premium booked in those two weeks. If agents gamed timing, net new premium = 0, but Vitality paid the 10% bonus on all shifted premium.
steps: If agents simply shift existing sales into Sweeps Week, total annual premium is unchanged
But Vitality pays an extra 10% bonus on the premium booked in those two weeks
This bonus has no incremental revenue offset, directly reducing profit margin
The chart confirms weeks surrounding Sweeps Week show below-100% ratios, consistent with agents pulling sales forward
math.answer: 'Sweeps Week' generated no net new premium; Vitality incurred extra commission expense with zero incremental revenue benefit.

questions.prompt: What is the likely impact of the new contests focused on acquiring new accounts?
questions.guidance: Even without a chart, a strong candidate recognizes that acquiring new customers is significantly more expensive than retaining or up-selling existing customers (higher agent effort, longer sales cycle, onboarding costs). Shifting contest emphasis from account retention/upsell (4 contests in 2008/09) to new account acquisition (0 retention contests, 4 new-account contests in 2010) will structurally increase the cost per dollar of premium, further compressing margins. This analysis does not require numbers but demonstrates commercial intuition about unit economics.

brainstorming.prompt: What other factors beyond sales contests could contribute to rising sales costs or declining profit margins at an insurance firm like Vitality?

categories.name: Agent workforce
ideas: Higher agent turnover driving recruiting and training costs
Increase in total headcount outpacing premium growth
Rising average commission rates negotiated by agents
Shift toward less productive new agents with lower close rates

categories.name: Sales process efficiency
ideas: Longer average sales cycles increasing cost per account
Higher administrative burden per sale reducing agent productivity
Geographic expansion into lower-density or harder-to-reach markets

categories.name: Product and customer mix
ideas: Shift toward lower-margin product lines (e.g., more disability vs. life)
Larger share of small employer accounts with lower premium density
Increased cross-sell complexity raising cost to serve

categories.name: Market and competitive dynamics
ideas: Competitive pressure requiring more aggressive discounting or higher commissions
Market maturation reducing organic referral volume
Regulatory changes increasing compliance costs within the sales process

categories.name: Contest and incentive design
ideas: Contest overlap causing double-payment on the same sale
Contests poorly aligned to profit-generating behaviors
Lack of a mechanism to audit or cap contest payouts

recommendation: Eliminate 'Sweeps Week' for 2011: the contest incentivizes agents to game enrollment timing rather than generate incremental premium, and its objective (total premium) is already covered by the standard commission structure
Repurpose the 'Sweeps Week' budget toward a contest targeting an activity not already rewarded by the base commission — for example, reactivating dormant accounts or retaining at-risk policyholders

Carefully review the new-account-focused contests before eliminating them, as Vitality may have a deliberate strategic rationale for a new-customer growth push; however, model the unit economics to confirm the CAC is justified by lifetime value
Reinstate some form of account-retention or upsell contest to counterbalance the 2010 shift away from keeping existing policyholders active
risks: If new-account growth is a deliberate strategic priority, cutting those contests could slow long-term premium growth
Agents who benefited from 'Sweeps Week' bonuses may react negatively to its elimination, potentially increasing turnover
Without a root-cause analysis of agent gaming behavior, a replacement contest could be gamed similarly if poorly designed
next_steps: Quantify the total bonus payout for 'Sweeps Week' in 2010 to confirm cost savings from elimination
Model customer lifetime value for new accounts acquired in 2010 vs. the incremental acquisition cost to assess whether the new-account contest investment will pay off over time
Audit remaining 2010 contests for similar gaming risks or duplicative incentive structures
Benchmark contest design best practices against comparable direct-sales insurance firms
